# AI and Young Workers: Why Companies Are Being Asked to Open the First Door

> **In short:** SAP says AI is already changing where careers begin. Stanford researchers found that 22- to 25-year-olds in the jobs most exposed to AI have fallen 19% behind those in less-exposed jobs, and SAP argues that companies should treat first jobs as their own concern.

Think about your first job, or the first job of someone you know. Those early roles usually taught you how work actually gets done: who to ask, how to phrase an email so someone answers it, which steps to never skip. Now imagine AI taking over many of those small tasks. That is the question SAP is raising.

## What the numbers show

SAP's announcement points to several studies. The first comes from researchers at Stanford, who used U.S. payroll data (the records employers keep on who is paid and for which jobs) to track AI's effect on employment. They found that young workers in jobs most exposed to AI, meaning jobs where AI can already handle a large share of the tasks, have fallen behind. Experienced workers in the same jobs showed no such gap. In other words, the change is hitting the starting line.

SAP also cites the International Labour Organization, which counts 257 million young people who are not in employment, education, or training. That is 9 million more than in 2023. Finally, it points to the World Bank Group, which expects around 1.2 billion young people in emerging economies (fast-growing countries with developing job markets) to reach working age over the next decade. Only about 420 million jobs are expected to be created there in that time.

SAP's point is that young people were struggling to find work before AI arrived. AI may make the gap wider, not create it.

## Why this is a business question

Entry-level jobs are where people build their first professional networks and learn the unwritten rules of work. Over time, those early hires become the experienced staff that companies depend on. SAP's argument is simple: if AI takes the tasks that used to train new people, a company might save time today but find it hard to grow its own talent in a few years.

SAP also says it has a direct stake. Its customers and partners need people who can run the technology they buy, and many of those people will be young professionals just starting out.

## Where companies can help

According to SAP, companies can do more through what they already do. Hiring from training programs they fund, buying from social enterprises (businesses that put social goals first), and lending staff experts to social innovators can all make a lasting difference, and they fit inside normal business operations.

SAP describes one example: the Youth Livelihoods Alliance, launched by UNICEF's Generation Unlimited with SAP, Accenture, and the Standard Chartered Foundation as founding partners. Its goal is to connect training to the next step. The alliance links partner programs into one route that runs from skills to recognized credentials (official records that you learned something) and then to a job. A digital platform called Yoma lets more than 1.3 million young people keep a verified record of what they have learned, so an employer does not have to take their word for it.

## Next stop: Heidelberg

SAP is also a partner of the UN Youth Townhall, hosted by the UN Youth Office from December 8 to 10, 2026, in Heidelberg, Germany. More than 1,000 young people are expected to meet leaders from governments, the UN, universities, and business to develop recommendations on AI, future skills, and work.

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life**: If you have a young person in your life who is looking for work, ask what they have practiced with AI tools and what they have built with them. Keeping a simple list of projects and courses you finished is a useful habit at any age.
- **For your business or work**: Look at the entry-level tasks on your team and ask whether they still teach people the work. If AI handles them, consider what new learning you could give a new hire instead.
- **If you're just getting started**: Think about the first tasks you were handed in your own job or studies. Write down what you learned from them. That list is a starting point for showing future employers what you can do.

## Wrap-up

AI is changing the first rung of many careers, and SAP argues that businesses should help keep that ladder in place. The numbers it cites show how large the challenge is, from the Stanford findings to the millions of young people outside work or study. Your next step is small: this week, talk with someone early in their career, or write down one thing you learned in your first job, and notice how much of it still matters today.
